source_lines.35: There are two finite one-step Markov decision processes with the same logged-data law under one behavior policy, but different target-policy values and different uniquely optimal actions. A finite one-step Markov decision process here has a finite state set, finite nonempty action sets, a finite reward set, and a probability mass on the next-state/reward pair for every state/action pair. Let the state set be $\{s_0,z\}$, the action sets be $A(s_0)=\{a,b\}$ and $A(z)=\{c\}$, the reward set be $\{-1,0,1\}$, and the horizon be $H=1$. In both processes, action $a$ at $s_0$ gives reward $0$ and moves to $z$, and action $c$ at $z$ gives reward $0$ and stays at $z$. In process $M_+$, action $b$ at $s_0$ gives reward $1$ and moves to $z$; in process $M_-$, it gives reward $-1$ and moves to $z$. The behavior policy chooses $a$ at $s_0$ with probability $1$, while the target policy chooses $b$ there with probability $1$; both policies choose $c$ at $z$ with probability $1$. Every behavior-generated logged trajectory is $(s_0,a,0,z)$ in both processes, so every sample size $n\ge1$ has the same logged-data law in $M_+$ and $M_-$. The target value is the expected one-step reward: it is $1$ in $M_+$ and $-1$ in $M_-$, and the unique value-maximizing initial action is $b$ in $M_+$ and $a$ in $M_-$. An estimator here is a real-valued function of the logged dataset; it is unbiased for a target value when its expectation under the logged-data law equals that value. Consequently, no such estimator can be unbiased for the target value in both processes, and no data-based action selector can identify the unique optimal initial action with certainty in both.
